newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Communists grumble before Russian budget debate.
newsitem.headline: Communists grumble before Russian budget debate.

text.p: Russian parliamentarians are due to discuss the final stage of the 1997 budget on Friday, but communist deputies hinted on Thursday the plan might never get on the agenda.
Communist Party leader Gennady Zyuganov said deputies wanted a detailed government schedule on payment of wage arrears and information on the media before agreeing to debate the budget.
"If those documents are not there tomorrow, we will not be able to debate the fourth reading of the budget," he said.
The communists are the largest faction in the State Duma lower house of parliament.
But other deputies said the budget would probably pass.

"It is tough to say how the Duma will behave," Interfax news agency quoted Alexander Shokhin, deputy speaker and a member of the pro-government Our Home Is Russia party, as saying. But "in any case" the budget would pass, he said.
The budget, rejected once by parliament, faced four months of debates and several government concessions to raise spending before deputies approved the first three readings last year.
It calls for a 3.5 percent budget deficit, by Russian calculations, on revenues of 434.4 trillion roubles ($77.3 billion) and expenditures of 529.8 trillion roubles.
The communists have sought additional protection for those Russians who lost out in market reforms in previous debates.
"It looks as though there are going to be some serious fights and long discussion," Viktor Ilyukhin, a senior communist deputy was quoted as saying by Itar-Tass news agency.

Ilyukhin, who led a parliamentary move to remove President Boris Yeltsin from office on health grounds, said his party would support the budget, as in previous readings, if the government continued to support a separate investment programme.

International bodies such as the International Monetary Fund, which resumed lending to Russia after a pause at the end of 1995, see passage of the bill as an indication that Russian economic planning is coming under control.
Russia has increased tax revenues that dropped to about 60 percent of target levels towards the middle of last year.
But Economy Minister Yevgeny Yasin, a leading reformer, said the government still spent too much -- 1997 government spending will rise to 45 percent of gross domestic product.
Economy Ministry figures quoted by Interfax put it at 38.8 percent in 1996.
Yasin predicted on Wednesday that the IMF would release a tranche of the $10 billion, three-year credit, but said Russia still faced a restructuring period before growth could begin.
Russia is still caught in a payment crisis from a web of debt between the government, workers and industry which Yasin told a recent news conference would slow growth this year.
"Financial stability was basically achieved (in 1996) and we can move on to the economic growth," Yasin said.
"But the present stage between stability and growth is the most difficult."
--Moscow Newsroom, +7095 941 8520 ($ = 5619 Russian Roubles)
